newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African maize harvest in full swing, yields high.
newsitem.headline: S.African maize harvest in full swing, yields high.

text.p: South Africa's maize harvest, set back by more than six weeks by unseasonal rain and extreme cold, is in full swing and early indications are that yields will be higher than expected, analysts said on Monday.
Physical and futures trading had started picking up last week, although yellow maize supplies were thin as farmers held back in the hope of securing higher prices.
"I think we have now reached the stage that we are in full harvesting. The maize is coming in fairly rapidly," said Giel van Zyl, general manager of the National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo).

Although poor weather conditions had caused some crop damage in the eastern Mpumalanga province, overall yields looked good. Some traders said they were hearing reports of yields at 5.5 tonnes per hectare compared to earlier expectations of between 3.5 and 4.2 tonnes.
The next official maize crop estimate is due on July 21. The June forecast was left unchanged from May at 7.660 million tonnes.
"The cash market is a lot more busy as there is more stock in the market and lots of maize in the silos as farmers look for buyers," a trader at an international commodity house said.
Traders said that producers were securing prices of between 500 and 520 rand a tonne ex-farm for white maize and around 490 rand for yellow.
Lower yellow prices had resulted in farmers looking for other means to market their maize, and some had turned to the South African Futures Exchange (Safex), which also allows physical delivery.

"It looks like the futures market is at the moment providing a possible alternative for farmers wishing to sell their spot maize," said Rod Blondin, general manager of Safex's agricultural market's division.

Trading on Safex, however, remained quiet last week as July white maize contracts hovered in a tight 585 to 590 rand band and yellow between 550 and 555 rand. Physical delivery took place on some 800 tonnes.
Traders said bottlenecks were starting to occur at South Africa's Durban port, as grain, delayed by the recent rains, started to roll in for export.

Shipping sources said earlier this month that around 250,000 tonnes of mostly white maize had been exported since the start of the new season on May 1. Most of that had been carryover from last year's crop.
Traders shrugged off concerns about El Nino, a weather phenomenon which can wreak havoc with climatic conditions. Scientists have said El Nino is likely to peak in December.
"It is too early to say whether it will happen. And El Nino concerns come up every year anyway," one trader said.

The most severe El Nino in recent memory took place in 1983 and caused blistering drought in Indonesia, South Africa, the Philippines and Australia while triggering floods in India and severe winter storms in California.
